scenario: AITA for insisting my daughter get a job even though we don't need her rent? | My 23 year old daughter Kirsty (not real name of course) lost her job in the city after testing positive for drugs. Her professional reputation has been ruined and she has no chance of getting into another big four company, and even smaller firms in her field (accounting) won't touch her. Kirsty was and is devastated and hasn't been doing much except crying in her room and going out clubbing with her friends. She has been like this for three months. and is starting to run low on money. Given that she has no chance of getting back into her career, I've been encouraging her to try to find some entry level work like retail/shop work or something like that. She sees it as a ''waste of her talents'' and thinks she's worth more than that. We have been arguing about it a lot. My wife Sarah and I don't need the rent from her, but at the same time she's been sitting here doing nothing for three months and asking for money from us. I told her that if she didn't make the effort to find another job she would have to find alternative living arrangements and she ran off crying. Sarah is mad at me. She agrees that working a job like that is a waste of Kirsty's ability. She did very well academically and was headhunted by her company as soon as she graduated. She had even been promoted to assistant manager not long before being sacked. Sarah had a go at me, saying that it wasn't fair for me to ''threaten'' her into getting a job that isn't good enough for her even though we don't need her rent money. I think I did the right thing. Happy to be a shoulder to cry on about the loss of her career, but not willing to let her spend the rest of her life living of us.

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the dad in this situation is being AITA (Ask if Too Angry) for insisting his daughter get a job even though they don't need her rent. Let me break this down step by step. First, the daughter, Kirsty, is 23 and lost her job in the city after testing positive for drugs. Her professional reputation is ruined, and she can't get another job in her field of accounting, even in smaller firms. She's been devastated for three months, crying and going out clubbing, and now she's running low on money. The dad wants her to get an entry-level job like retail or shop work, but she sees it as a waste of her talents and thinks she's worth more than that. They've been arguing a lot about this. The dad says they don't need her rent money, but he's not willing to let her spend the rest of her life living off them. He told her she'd have to find alternative living arrangements if she doesn't make an effort to find a job, which made her cry. His wife, Sarah, is mad at him, saying it's not fair to threaten her into getting a job that's not good enough for her, especially since they don't need the rent. So, is the dad being AITA? Let's think about this. On one hand, the dad is trying to encourage his daughter to take some responsibility for her situation. She's been unemployed for three months, and while it's understandable that she's devastated, sitting around and not doing anything isn't healthy. Getting a job, even if it's not in her field, could help her regain some sense of purpose and independence. It might also help her save some money and avoid running out of funds. On the other hand, the dad is threatening her with eviction, even though they don't need her rent. That might come across as harsh, especially since she's already going through a tough time. It could make her feel unsupported and increase her stress levels. Plus, Sarah, his wife, thinks it's unfair to push her into a job that doesn't match her skills or ambitions. Maybe there's a middle ground. Instead of threatening her, the dad could have had a more supportive conversation about the importance of finding some kind of work, even if it's temporary. He could have offered to help her look for jobs or explore other options, like further education or training in a different field. Threatening her might have made her feel cornered and less likely to take his advice. Also, considering her age and the fact that she's just starting her career, it's a tough situation. She might feel like her whole future is ruined, and that's a lot to handle. The dad's approach might have been too harsh, and he could have been more empathetic to her feelings. In conclusion, while the dad's intention to encourage responsibility is understandable, his method of threatening her might be seen as AITA. A more supportive and collaborative approach could have been more effective in helping her move forward.
